name: lexical-core (number parsing and formatting)
baseline: std's str::parse::<f64> and Display for floats
verdict_reason: The README calls lexical the currently fastest Rust number formatter and parser, but dtoa-benchmark puts zmij (8.5 ns) and teju (21.4 ns) ahead of lexical (24.4 ns) for f64 formatting. For float parsing std has used Eisel-Lemire since 1.55 and trails lexical by only 1.09x-1.51x; the README itself points users to std for floats and to itoa for integers. Against std's float Display it is 2.8x-2.9x faster.
tier_reason: Public benchmarks with CPU and Rust version stated (dtoa-benchmark; fast-float2's simple-bench).
claimed_speedup: f64 formatting 24.4 ns vs libcore 68.8 ns (2.82x) and 22.0 vs 63.9 ns (2.90x); zmij 8.5 ns, teju 21.4 ns. f64 parsing on i7-14700K, Rust 1.81: canada 10.62 vs 11.59 ns, bi 26.40 vs 35.92 ns; on EPYC 7763, Rust 1.83: mesh 8.41 vs 12.72 ns (1.09x-1.51x across datasets, derived from page data)
workload: Formatting: random f64 at 1-17 significant digits (dtoa-benchmark). Parsing: ns per f64 on canada, mesh, uniform, big integer, %de%d and reciprocal datasets (fast-float2 README).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9975WX and Apple M4 Max (formatting); Intel i7-14700K and AMD EPYC 7763 (parsing)
os: Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2) and Ubuntu 24.04.1 for the parsing tables
one_liner: Configurable number parsing and formatting; 2.8x faster than std at printing floats, but no longer the fastest and only 1.1x-1.5x ahead at parsing.
how_it_is_fast: Float parsing uses Eisel-Lemire with a slower exact fallback, the approach this author ported into std for Rust 1.55. Writing goes into a caller-provided byte buffer instead of through core::fmt::Formatter, and unused conversions are compiled out by feature flags.
use_it_when: Parsing number formats std rejects or treats differently (digit separators, other languages' syntax, JSON-strict rules) via its format options
Partial parsers that return the number of bytes consumed
skip_it_when: Plain f64 parsing: std's from_str is within 1.1x-1.5x since Rust 1.55
Fastest float printing: zmij is 2.9x faster
Integer formatting: the README itself suggests itoa
caveats: Parsing numbers come from fast-float2's README, written by lexical's own author
The 'Apple M1 (macOS)' table in fast-float2's README lists an AMD EPYC CPU, a copy-paste error, so that table is not used here
lexical's README metrics are chart images
tradeoffs: RUSTSEC-2023-0086 and RUSTSEC-2023-0055 (soundness) affected versions before lexical-core 1.0 and lexical 7.0
Large feature surface and compile time unless features are trimmed

evidence.quote: Lexical is the currently fastest Rust number formatter and parser

If you want a minimal, performant float parser, recent versions of the Rust standard library should be [sufficient](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/86761). For high-performance integer formatters, look at [itoa](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/).
The following results are measured on a 2025 AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9975WX and 2024 Apple M4 Max, each using Rust 1.97.0:
- CPU: Intel i7-14700K 3.40GHz - OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2) - Rust: 1.81
- CPU: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor 3.20GHz - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.1 - Rust: 1.83
